opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and one I think about a lot. I'm cautiously optimistic, but I think NetHack is going to be much harder for large language models than people might initially expect.

On the one hand, there's a lot going for LLMs here. NetHack has been around for decades, and there's an enormous amount of human knowledge about it on the internet: the NetHack wiki, spoilers, forum discussions, ascension posts where people walk through their whole game. A model trained on web-scale data has almost certainly absorbed a good chunk of that. So in principle it "knows" things like: don't eat a cockatrice corpse, pray when your HP is low but not too often, Elbereth scares most monsters, and so on. That's exactly the kind of prior knowledge a pure reinforcement learning agent starting from scratch doesn't have, and it's a big part of why NetHack has been so hard for RL.

On the other hand, knowing facts about the game and actually playing it well over tens of thousands of steps are very different things. NetHack is extremely long-horizon. A successful game can take on the order of 50,000 or more actions, and a single mistake, sometimes made hundreds of turns earlier, can doom you. It's also procedurally generated and partially observable, so you can't just memorize a trajectory. You need to keep track of what you've identified, which items you've seen, where the stairs were, what your intrinsics are, all while reasoning about risk in a very stochastic environment. That's precisely where current models tend to struggle: long-term memory, consistent planning, and not drifting or forgetting the state of the world.

What we saw in the NetHack Challenge at NeurIPS was quite telling. The best systems weren't deep RL agents; they were symbolic, hand-engineered bots that encoded a lot of human expertise. And even those were nowhere near ascending reliably. When people have plugged language models into NetHack, you get agents that can do sensible-looking things locally, but overall progress through the dungeon is still pretty limited.

So my view is that LLMs are probably a necessary ingredient, because they bring that world knowledge and the ability to read and reason about text, which NetHack is full of. But on their own, I don't think prompting a model is going to solve it. You'll likely need to combine them with things like better memory and state tracking, the ability to learn from interaction rather than just from pretraining, and some form of open-ended self-improvement, where the agent keeps generating its own challenges and gets better over time. That's actually why I love NetHack as a benchmark: it's cheap to run, but it's not going to be saturated quickly, and it really stress-tests exactly the capabilities we'd want from more general agents.

r001.rationale: The response says current models struggle with long-term memory, planning, and state tracking, and that prompting a model alone is not going to solve NetHack.

r002.rationale: It identifies procedural generation and partial observability, the need to track locations such as stairs, and limited progress through the dungeon as obstacles to effective exploration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a really interesting question, and I'd say I'm cautiously optimistic, but with a lot of caveats. When we organized the NetHack Challenge at NeurIPS, the thing that struck everyone was that the winning entries were all symbolic bots, hand-crafted rule-based systems, and they outperformed the neural approaches by a wide margin. So even with reinforcement learning at scale, the learning-based agents were really quite far behind.

Now, large language models change the picture in one important way. NetHack has this enormous body of human knowledge around it, the NetHack wiki, strategy guides, decades of forum discussions, the source code itself. And a lot of what makes the game hard is precisely that you need that knowledge. You need to know that you shouldn't eat a cockatrice corpse, that you should pray when your hit points are low but not too frequently, that certain items need to be identified before you use them. A language model pretrained on the internet has absorbed a lot of this already, which is something an RL agent trained from scratch simply doesn't have access to. So in principle, you get a prior that would otherwise take millions of environment interactions to acquire, if you could acquire it at all.

But there are some real obstacles. The first is that NetHack is a very long-horizon problem. A successful game can involve tens of thousands of steps, and the decisions you make early on, like what you do with your starting inventory or which branches of the dungeon you explore, have consequences much later. Current language models are not particularly good at that kind of long-horizon planning and credit assignment, and just prompting them to act step by step tends to fall apart over those time scales. The second is grounding. The model might know in the abstract what a floating eye is, but it needs to connect that to what it's actually seeing in the observation and act accordingly in real time, and that connection is surprisingly brittle. And the third is that the game is stochastic and partially observable, so you can't just memorize a plan, you have to adapt constantly.

So what I expect is that language models will be a very useful component, maybe as a source of knowledge or high-level goals that guide a lower-level policy, or as a way to shape rewards and curricula, rather than being the whole solution out of the box. The thing I find most exciting is that NetHack is really a benchmark for open-endedness. It tests whether a system can keep learning and adapting in a world that is too big to enumerate. If language models can meaningfully help there, that tells us something quite deep about how far these models are from general problem solving. And if they can't, that's equally informative. Either way, I think it's one of the best testbeds we have right now.

r001.rationale: The response says current language models struggle with long-horizon planning and expects them to guide a lower-level policy rather than serve as the whole solution out of the box, indicating they will not solve the challenge alone in their current form.

r002.rationale: The response mentions choosing dungeon branches, but does not identify difficult exploration itself as an obstacle.

astra-6.text:
I’m optimistic, but I think NetHack is a much harder test than it might look at first. It’s a game presented through text, so you might think it’s a natural fit for a large language model. But knowing things about NetHack and being able to play it reliably are very different capabilities.

You have to make decisions over a very long horizon, under partial observability, and mistakes can be irreversible. You need to explore, manage resources, and adapt your strategy to whatever the game throws at you. A model might give you a perfectly sensible explanation of what you should do and then fail to execute that strategy consistently.

So I think language models can provide a useful starting point, particularly in bringing prior knowledge into the agent. The interesting question is how you combine that with learning from interaction—an agent that can discover when its assumptions are wrong and improve through experience. I’m less convinced that simply asking a larger model what key to press next will get us all the way there.

r001.rationale: The response expresses optimism and doubts that a larger model alone will be enough, but it does not clearly judge that current large language models will not solve NetHack.

r002.rationale: It says an agent must explore, but does not clearly identify difficult exploration as an obstacle.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m excited about the possibility, but I think NetHack is a much harder test than it might first appear. It’s a turn-based game with a relatively small action space, yet succeeding requires long-term planning, exploration, and dealing with situations where a mistake can end your run. You have to connect decisions now to consequences much later.

Language models offer an interesting advantage because they can potentially draw on descriptions of the game and reason about strategies. But knowing a strategy and reliably executing it over a long game are very different things. You need to keep track of what’s happened, recognize when your plan no longer applies, and adapt.

So I’m optimistic, particularly about combining language models with agents that learn through interaction. But I wouldn’t take fluent explanations of how to play as evidence that we’ve solved the challenge. The important test is whether an agent can actually win consistently.

r001.rationale: The response is optimistic about the possibility of solving NetHack but does not say that current large language models will fail to solve it.

r002.rationale: It says success requires exploration and frames that demand as part of why NetHack is a hard test.
